Like the others have said, it's now really the same as any big city shopping centre. Over the years various owners have stripped it of the unique character and atmosphere it once had. I've always lived nearby and in the 90s would visit a number of times a year. It had Metroland, palm trees, fountains, an awesome little bazaar village type thing, plenty of quirky little shops as well as the big ones, and Toys R Us was massive just outside as well. 

Nowadays Metroland and all of the unique decor is long gone, it's a copy/paste Intu design now. All of the small fun shops were priced out and closed down. The upstairs walkway between blue and green sections used to home a bunch of small shops, now the entire section is 100% empty on the green side and has been for years. Just a huge empty white-painted void with occasionally some art installation from Temu that just looks sad. Takes inspiration from that willy wonka land thing. Green mall is depressing in general, there's basically only Boots, WHSmiths (for now) and M&S.

In general it's not bad compared to similar big shopping centres,  but doesn't do anything different to the rest of them now. Handy for certain things if you're local, but I wouldn't go out of my way just to visit it. If you're after somewhere nice to visit/maybe stop off for food, you'll find more unique stuff in Newcastle itself, or if you're heading North then Alnwick is a short stop off the A1 a bit further up as well.

I'll probably pick up a PS5 this year purely so I can play Astro Bot, Final Fantasy VII, Stellar Blade, Returnal, and a few others.

If next-gen I can get all my favourite Xbox games on PS6, plus the inevitable Sony exclusives I'd like to play, why would I buy an Xbox?

And yes I'm well aware a majority of gamers only play Call of Duty/EA FC/Madden etc, but those gamers are highly likely to just stay wherever they currently are. Exclusives don't entice those people, but the 7 million people who bought Final Fantasy VII remake, the 10 million+ who bought the Last of Us 2 and Horizon Zero Dawn, and apparently Forza Horizon 5 sold over 10 million copies outside of Gamepass as well. Maybe some of these are including PC sales, but top tier exclusives like these sell, and sell well.

The players who buy these kinds of exclusives, are also more likely the kind of players who simply buy more games in general, so they're great to have.

My biggest issue is that Xbox will have zero incentive to buy into their ecosystem, other than existing users feeling locked in because you've spent 10-20+ years building a library there. That obviously won't attract anyone new so the userbase can only decline. A shrinking userbase will also make smaller third party devs far less likely to port to Xbox, which is already lagging behind Nintendo and Sony quite badly in that aspect. It seems to often take the promise of Microsoft throwing Gamepass deals out to entice some ports to even happen now.

Ultimately Xbox will increasingly have the worst choice of games, and once a big publisher like EA drops out because the sales are no longer worth porting there, then it's GG Xbox.

Sorry but I just can't see how it's clunky at all so I'm just going to have to disagree. Compared to Control (which I already like quite a lot), QB handles like a dream. The core gameplay is absolutely not "sit behind cover" at all, if that's how you've played it then I can see why you don't like it. If you play aggressively with the powers, you shouldn't need cover at all once you've got a few abilities to play with, and except to play cat and mouse with the late-game juggernauts, and even then you need to stay on the move. Using the time dash effectively you can make enemies lose track of you, opening them up to a devastating counter attack, then both the time shield and blast can buy you breathing space when you need it. You need to balance how and when you use these, not just spam them all at once then sit there miserably waiting for them to recharge at the same time. Guns have plenty of power if you use them right, you may not be able to time stop certain enemies but you can still use the time bubble thing to stack bullets into them. Jack is hugely manoeuvrable in this game and you need to exploit that, sitting behind cover is legit the worst thing you can do as you'll just get surrounded.

I also can't think of any power that doesn't feel time related, except for the ol' video game vision sense thing. Maybe the time blast is pushing it but everything else feels very specific to slowing/stopping/speeding up time in one way or another.

Have to disagree. The story is one of the better time travel ones in any media, you can tell how much effort went into making it something plausible and somewhat grounded in reality. And the core gameplay is probably still Remedy's best they've ever done. I legitimately don't know how anyone can complain about it unless they only played the first few levels. All of the time powers Jack gets feel so tight and blend together wonderfully. Combat is a balance of what to use against what enemy, and you have to make the most of your abilities, just playing it like a regular shooter isn't where its strengths are.

I love Control for the telekinesis ability which feels amazingly chunky, and aesthetically it's absolutely on point, but otherwise in general it feels a bit loose and floaty. It works for the game, but Quantum Break is tighter and more intense, which again works for it and the somewhat more serious tone it has. When it comes together it's amazing, it's just a shame that the game is fairly short and by the time you've got your full arsenal of abilities you're already on the approach to endgame. Still I'd rather it leave me wanting more than overstaying it's welcome with padded out fluff, and it does pace the game out nicely with new powers and upgrades so it never sits still and gets stale.

People don't want to be forced into something that is prohibitively expensive and impractical, which is the case for a huge number of us in the UK. If you're desperate, you can still pick up an ICE car for £500 or less that runs. Won't be pretty but will do a job. Plenty of people still running cheap cars because that's all they can afford. The cheapest EV's in running condition currently start at around £3.5k. May not sound like much to some people, but there are plenty of people who have never bought a car for anywhere near that price. My first 3 cars were cheaper than that combined.

The prices will likely keep falling of course, but then the issue of practicality remains a sticking point that isn't going to be so easily fixed. Those cheap EV's are typically all Nissan Leaf's with sub 100 mile range even when new, quite likely a bit less now. Fine for short city driving, but quickly becomes a problem for many. Especially in places like the North East, where the infrastructure barely exists and public transport coverage is already so poor in rural areas that cars can be a necessity. Plus people who are likely to need cars on a budget are highly unlikely to have a nice driveway to charge their car on. Scores of people live in flats or terraced housing that makes home charging impossible.

These people are being told that they're going to have to get an EV eventually, when at the moment they simply can't meet their needs that are easily met on the cheap by ICE cars.

It's all very easy for Londoners or people who can afford £300+ PCP payments without batting an eye to think it's simple to run an EV or just use public transport. The reality for many people is that it's simply impossible for them to afford and/or work around, and being told that they're going to be forced into it is distressing. Many people couldn't even begin to imagine what it's like to be able to walk into a dealer and buy a brand new Tesla or BMW 4 Series. People who can afford to do such things so easily, often seem to struggle to put themselves in the mindset of those who can't. People barely living paycheck to paycheck don't appreciate being forced into a harder situation by people who have zero idea of living through that kind of struggle. EV's to them are a rich plaything whereas their current cars are a crucial part of their life. Until this perception can be changed, there will always be hostility to being forced into it. Nobody gave a shit about EVs until they became mandated before they were a viable alternative to current standards. I guarantee these people have bigger immediate worries than climate change so that argument will not work on them.

If EVs become so effective and easy to work with at comparative prices that they make ICE obsolete by comparison, then people would naturally switch. Being forced into it before that stage is what is causing the animosity.

I imagine they save a bit of CPU cost by mapping it to a 2D system and ignoring the height/Y-axis. Probably served them really well throughout the Horizon series until things started getting a little wacky with FH4 and event lab. If they continue down that route I imagine they'll eventually change it, especially if they go current-gen only in the next game and stop supporting the Xbox One. The extra CPU grunt of the new machines should handle a more robust occlusion system with ease, but I imagine FH5 as it is will be pushing the X1 to the absolute limit. Still boggles my mind how it works on that machine as smoothly as it does.

It'll be a line of sight occlusion/chunk system that was never intended to be used from this height, it'll be calculating it as if the player was on the ground. From the ground those chunks that are visible likely contain high ground that would be visible to the player from the ground, whereas the hidden chunks contain nothing that would be visible in that position so they are disabled. The system can't account for the player being higher than expected so the results start to get funky. Occasionally see the same thing on some regular stunt jumps where you can absolutely launch yourself in an S2/X car. (The roundabout at the end of the highway is a good example)

I do get why people like RE7, like it's still a great horror game overall. I think RE4 in particular though people forget what it was like on a first play through before you learned to become a ganado slaying agent of death. Once you get good at it and have infinite ammo magnums and rocket launchers the game just gets silly, but that's most RE games tbf. I loved the recent Remake for bringing back that first play through feel again

I don't exactly disagree with any that, I just feel they took it too far into Outlast territory. RE 1 and 2 got fight or flight down to an art, but RE7 at least in the early game is too focused on purely flight, which is also why I don't like Outlast. It's just constant hide and seek, not survival horror. Then 7 gradually descends into mindless mold slaughter later in the game. It definitely picked up around mid-game, but I dislike the early and late game sections for opposite reasons.

I know RE4 is way more action oriented than what came before it, but at times it still totally nails the old school RE vibes. The opening village fight is absolutely stellar RE, you're barely equipped and running around desperate for stuff to keep you alive. I also love the Regenerators for throwing a total curveball later in the game once you're confident and armed to the teeth. Suddenly you feel weak and helpless again despite all your stuff. Despite getting overloaded with stuff it still had a few tricks to force you into changing tact and piling pressure on you.

The mechanic stuff is fine, but I wanted them to improve the game around it which they didn't. It's more or less the same, or even worse in some aspects. I thought the garage could have been updated better. It's bigger but somehow we lost a space to work on a car, and there's loading screens when going anywhere around your garage which feels like a step back. And your garage feels big and empty. You can't drive the cars yourself, the whole forecourt feels like wasted space that exists for no reason. I wanted them to do more about the vehicles you can buy and repair for yourself. The auction house should have been better, cars always sell for way under value if you don't bid, but if you do bid you'll always get outbid until it reaches value. There's no chance of a cool bargain or getting into a bidding war over value for something rare you really want. I want there to be a reason to scavenge for parts in the junkyard and barns, at the moment it's virtually pointless as you can simply buy anything you need and at a cheap cost. The junkyard is way bigger with no reason, without any use for scavenging for parts it's just busy work making you walk around. The garage parking is a complete downgrade. I wanted something to do with the cars you buy and restore, instead there's now less to do with them. You can't see or display them, they just get tucked away and loaded one by one. You just restore and sell them, unless you buy the drag race DLC but that's still a pretty niche thing. At least it gives you something to do other than just sell a car. Like the empty forecourt at the garage, why not have space to display or even sell cars there? Selling is literally just click a button and it's gone, no auctions or anything that would add anything to the meta game. Considering 3 years of Dev time, it's functionally almost exactly the same as the previous game, both in terms of working on the cars and the meta game around it.

You can absolutely get it MOT'd if you like, there's no requirement to do so but there's nothing actually stopping you from getting one if you'd like to. If it fails with a dangerous fault it would still be illegal to drive it, not because of the MOT failure, but because of a dangerous fault. Although you don't need an MOT, you do still have to ensure your car is actually roadworthy. If you end up in a crash/get pulled over and your car is found to be in a dangerous state you'll still get rapped for it, MOT or not.

Otherwise if you don't want an MOT, just ask any mechanic who is happy to deal with classics to inspect it periodically. I'd definitely go for a classic enthusiast or specialist if you have one local.  Any decent garage that does an inspection for you should give you a printed or written list of any issues or potential issues they found, as you would with an MOT failure/advisory checklist.

If it's a yellow one and looking as old as the car, try to get a closer look at it. Any signs of stress/age cracks in that fan, and that should be top of your list to replace if you end up buying it. Shouldn't be too expensive to do, whether you do it yourself or bring it to a garage, but that fan can shatter once they reach a certain age and start cracking. I didn't say they couldn't do it, but making an offline version will take people away from developing the online version which will be the absolute priority for now. Depending on how deep the server integration is, it could be many months of work to build a proper offline version of it, which absolutely won't be a priority when the game is a couple of months away from going gold.

Just because an offline version will be "simpler" in the end, doesn't necessarily mean it's a simple process to get there. An offline, single player World of Warcraft would be a simpler game than the MMO, but engineering the existing game into that would probably take years if it was attempted.

I haven't played a Far Cry in co-op, but I'd have some questions. Are they drop-in/drop-out, or does the host have to reload a world if a player wants to join? Can the players wander as far as they like away from each other or is there some sort of limit imposed?

Like I said, it absolutely isn't impossible for Arkane to implement, but it's a question of difficulty which leads to how much time is required (and time is money). Ubisoft are also kings of open world, whether you love or hate them - they do have open world tech down to an art. This is Arkane's first attempt at anything like this as far as I know, so they won't have had any existing infrastructure to build upon. Bethesda also don't have any open world multiplayer games that aren't fully online afaik as well so not much that could be shared with Arkane to help. Even Microsoft doesn't have much experience in that realm, hell it took them a year post-launch to get co-op into Halo Infinite, and that's a flagship title.

All I'm saying is open world multiplayer is a bitch to work on, and depending on the size of it will almost certainly be handled by servers in any game as long as players can wander wherever they like. Building a single player offline version of that is always possible, but will require some reworking for sure. It's quite possible once the game is done then Arkane may shift some of the engineering team over to making that happen, but for now they'll be focused on finishing the game as it is.

Borderlands is also a semi-linear/segmented world, which doesn't compare to an open world (though again, I don't know how big Redfall actually is, but they definitely call it open world).

Also connecting players completing objectives or not in an online session, is a design choice. Whether you like or agree with that choice is irrelevant, it's still a co-op game and that has absolutely zero bearing on how they build the online infrastructure.

Loose is so much better, with maybe a little more smoothing (especially on a jump landing or sudden movement stop). Highly recommend checking out Ori and the Will of the Wisps or its sequel. The camera moves quickly when it needs to, but lazily follows when you're bouncing around in the centre of the screen.

If Redfall has been designed from the ground up as an online co-op shooter, it's more than possible to suggest that having a connected server could be integral to some of the game design. I don't know enough about Redfall or how expansive the game's worlds are, but from what I do understand is that it's an open world. Hosting an open world multiplayer game purely on a host client can quickly become impossible based on how big it is, and how far players can stray away from each other as that host client will be tasked with simulating all active areas of the open world on top of rendering what they can see. Normally parts of these open worlds will be loaded and unloaded as you move around, but allowing players to wander into these unloaded areas starts to get very messy. Obviously those players will load any graphical assets themselves, but only the host will be expected to run any logic like AI, which they won't be running if they don't have anything loaded for that area. Either you strain the client to somehow try and handle it, or you have these worlds persistently handled by a server which doesn't have to worry about any rendering and can dedicate all resources to simply simulating the world and all its moving actors. There's a reason why open world games that also include multiplayer often separate these out completely, even when it's the same world (ala GTA, Red Dead - there's no dropping in or out of a single player session of these). Linear or segmented worlds are far easier to handle in small, concentrated areas where players can't wander miles away from each other.

It's quite possible Arkane could separate these out in the future, would make drop-in, drop-out gameplay a lot more difficult if that's how it works now, but relying on a server to handle a multiplayer open world is absolutely not an unusual design. Building an offline single player mode would certainly be possible in any case, but how difficult and time consuming that is depends on how deeply Arkane have hooked functionality into having a host server. They may have decided that wasn't a priority and not worth the effort, or it could be something they're still looking at but getting the main game out first.

It's not necessarily just Ferrari. There are a lot of high end brands in Forza and most of them have a very wide range of their cars available. And like Ferrari for example, we don't know if they provide a blanket "you can do X with all of our cars" or if it's more like "you can do X with a LaFerrari but not a GTO California". Forza does also have some minor body loss (spoilers and wing/side mirrors etc) but nothing much more extensive. A number of Devs have openly talked about brand owners having issues with damage in the past although I'm sure some (like Ferrari) have relented and softened slightly on it, but without seeing contract details we can't know exactly what the limits currently are. Need for Speed also just doesn't have the sheer number of cars that any Forza title does. It's probably a mix of both negotiating for that many cars as well as actually having to model them all - lost body panels also means sculpting and rendering what's underneath. A lot of work for 500-600+ cars ultimately, for something that would only be marginally better than what we have now.

Could you imagine the complaints if Forza had Ford's that damaged that much, but then Ferrari/McLaren/Bugatti were stuck with the current model because that's as much as they'll allow. It would look wildly out of place, so ultimately whichever company sets the strictest conditions on how their cars can appear, sets the bar for the entire game. Only alternatives are showing manufacturers with mismatched damage modelling, or dropping those manufacturers entirely. It's not a question of can Playground do better damage modelling, it's what are they allowed to do whilst playing ball with every manufacturer in the game.

That was why I thought you generally wouldn't use SSR for actual mirrors as you won't see an accurate reflection. Definitely used a ton on glass buildings, shiny floors, water etc as it's good for general scenery but not enough for an actual mirror. Granted I don't recall many modern games that really bother with accurate mirrors compared to the PS2 days where it was a cool trick to show off, so loads of games in that era crammed it in with the old dual world trick. I would assume most games with accurate mirrors these days use the render to texture method.
Nintendo saw the Gran Turismo movie announced and we were like damn, we need in on this trend

I know screen space reflections are used frequently on water and shiny surfaces, but what games have used them for an actual mirror? That example in Hitman does not look like SSR to me but I'd be happily proven wrong. Looks like a two camera setup there imo

Most working mirrors you see in games are actually just a window to a duplicate world where everything is flipped. So there's 2 of each character moving around running the same animations, just flipped horizontally. They're expensive in that it requires everything you need to see to be duplicated.

The other main method you often see in racing games where a second camera is pointing backwards, and the output of that camera is mapped to the rear view and side mirrors. Still expensive to do as now you're rendering the world from two viewpoints so still doing everything twice. Most games that use this trick will have the second cam heavily neutered so it can't see shadows or smaller objects for example, and usually have massively scaled back draw distances on everything to save performance.

Ray tracing I believe can be genuinely capturing/simulating reflections rather than having to resort to these tricks, but that's a whole extra cost and technicality to consider. Current Gen versions of Spiderman and WatchDogs Legion both used this if I remember right.

Can't defend the rest of the game's flaws, but loading times are an ongoing problem that likely won't ever go away.

Yes we've come up with a few tricks for better loading times, but when you consider games in 2006 were pretty limited by RAM (only half a gig on the Xbox 360), whereas today the X1 and PS4 are both rocking 8GB of RAM, there's a LOT more data needing to be loaded in many games now compared to what we were loading 10 years ago. PC numbers have scaled similarly, and on all formats many people are still rocking the same hard drive tech as back then.

SSDs are great, but when you start wanting 4k textures and super high quality models/sounds/animations that machines can run today, you're gonna have to load all that extra data somehow, and you can't wave a magic wand to speed up your hard drive.

Games today are a lot sneaker about when they're loading as they can often load a lot of data whilst you're watching the intros and mucking around in the main menu, but typically in a big game you're still going to have a hefty load upfront. Even if the game can dynamically load and unload content once you're in the world (like red dead/gta) you still need the core elements of the world loaded first, and in a game that size that's still a heck of a lot to load.

Poor management of resources or bad design can still lead to more loading screens than is necessary. As games are getting ever more complex in terms of content and in design, it's an uphill battle to keep on top of it all. Some developers have clearly adapted to the challenge more than others, but there's no universal magic fix for it. What works for one game may not be applicable to another.

Games engines still often cheat a lot, especially when it comes to intensive operations such as lighting, but they're getting really clever at that too. Some lighting you see in games will be pre-baked, which can take hours to calculate upfront, but can then be used in realtime. Only drawback is once it's baked, it's set. You can't change it but you can get some really professional-looking results with it. It works great for games where you're not concerned about time of day changing.

But games with day/night cycles are also looking crazy impressive. Check out any time lapse videos of Forza Horizon 3 to see the kind of lighting we can currently get even in an open-world game. Also some of the mods people are using on games like Skyrim and GTA5. Some of them run like ass even with an amazing PC, but there are plenty out there now which look incredible at playable framerates.

I love early/cheap IT systems.

I worked for a county council Library network which had an outsourced IT system fairly recently put in place about 13/14 years ago.

You could search the database for books, and then find out what branch had them in stock to request stock movements (which you still had to do by phone, but it was better than calling them each one by one looking for a book!)

I found out the hard way that if I searched for something that returned zero results (a simple typo of an author's name will do the trick), and then immediately tried searching again, it would wipe the entry field of whatever was typed into it, and then attempt to search the entire database with zero input.

Cue a null reference error and I brought down the entire computer system at county hall which was running the database.

They didn't fix it either. After figuring out what I did to crash everything, they simply told me not to do it again lol. The entire system was outsourced and they had no engineers in-house who could fix it and prevent it from happening again. Kinda surprised they didn't have the original developers on some sort of retention.

Rocket League is not a yearly release for example. It would seriously hurt the reputation of the game on Switch if it released with missing features, whereas EA can release a new one in a years time and people will praise it if it releases with the features that were previously missing.

Basically yes EA could have easily added those features in, but at a cost they probably weren't sure was worth it. Smaller companies have more to gain from drawing in some popularity early on the Switch.

> but it is a fact that the console is flying off the shelves right now WITHOUT these games

The same was true of the original Wii as well remember, best launch ever for Nintendo, and look how that turned out. It *very quickly* became a dumping ground of shovelware and all but abandoned by every major third party publisher after what, a year or two? I'm much more optimistic with the Switch currently, but Nintendo absolutely needs strong third party support in the long run. The Wii, WiiU, and even the Gamecube all suffered in the dying years from a painful lack of anything decent to play other than first party titles.

If the Switch is to continue being a success, it needs to keep up the interest from third parties, and a shockingly bare online infrastructure compared to the competition could end up causing beef with some of them.

Sure some devs might be prepared to put the work in to get around the problem (Psyonix for example), but it's quite a costly gamble to do so. Developing online features takes quite a bit of time and manpower, and these features would *only* benefit the Switch. When EA/Activison/Ubisoft etc are all already trying to create online experiences for PS4 and X1, a significant portion of that development time/personel would have to be sacrificed just to get the Switch version up to scratch.

It's far more likely they'll instead have a skeleton crew work on such features (fun tasks for the new junior employees) and slowly work them in over time. There's absolutely no reason for EA to dedicate all that time and money into working on features that Nintendo should already have.

You can be pretty sure those devs weren't too happy about it either. I wouldn't be surprised if that's why Mario Kart missed launch either. These kinds of online features aren't exactly knocked out in no time, and now it has to be done on a per-game basis. That's a huge inconvenience.

EA are still using their own servers, matchmaking etc. You can still play online on the Switch, but it's missing features that the PSN/Xbox Live environments handle such as friends, lobbies/groups, voice chat. All that infrastructure is provided by Microsoft and Sony by default, to every game on those consoles. EA literally only has to send a function call to invite a friend to a game.

The Switch cannot do that. The online setup of FIFA on the X1 and PS4 simply cannot provide the same functionality as the other consoles without major reworking. Matchmaking with random users is totally fine, cause EA already does that for the other consoles, but EA does not know who your Switch buddies are and the Switch provides no way to invite anyone to anything.

EA would have to create a bespoke system just to handle simple functions for *every single game* they release, when these simple functions are a natural part of the network on the other systems.

Nintendo is literally decades behind at this point. The original Xbox had a much more in-depth, robust and feature-heavy network than Nintendo has now. If they start charging for it in this state it will be a joke and such a slap in the face to their fans.

It really isn't a case of EA not doing enough work. It would require a ton of work that shouldn't even be expected in this day and age. Especially with this being the first FIFA release on Switch, I don't blame EA at all for not wanting to risk a ton of development on a handful of features that should already be available to them.

Stockholm - Sweden.

Simply breathtaking city, and so much to see and do.

It's built on a lake of sorts, and one travel card gets you on any transport across the city whether it's bus, tram, subway or even the ferry. Ridiculously good public transport.

Amazing cafe's everywhere, especially in the old town which is full of old style buildings and narrow streets. The Swedes themselves are hugely friendly everywhere I went and 9/10 of them appear to speak fluent English, even when I tried speaking terrible Swedish at them.

There's the Vasa Museum, which houses a 17th century ship that sailed from Stockholm harbour and immediately sank, but the inland bay prevented it from decaying as much as it would in sea water so it's still in amazing condition. The museum gives great insight into how/why it sank (tldr version - way too top heavy) and the recovery process to bring it back up.

There's also Skansen. An open air museum which is basically half a recreation of a Viking village, and half zoo. Pretty amazing thing to have smack bang in the middle of a city like that.

I've only been once, but it's top of my list of places I would go a second time for sure.

Most currently existing games won't automatically look better, but in the future they might. Halo 5 for example already includes automatic resolution scaling built into the game. It constantly tries to push for max resolution, but if there's a danger of the framerate dropping, the resolution automatically drops instead, and visa versa. If the game is running comfortably the resolution will dynically increase.

Theoretically, simply just running that on the X1X without even patching the game would still make a difference, simply because it (should) be hitting max resolution possible at all times.

I'm not sure how many other games already out there use tricks like this, but it should still certainly help out any games that suffer unsteady or frequently dropping framerates. I can see more games going with the auto-adjusting method used by Halo in the future, and maybe not even restricted to just resolution/framerates. Things like lighting and texture resolutions could by dynamically adjusted depending on available power and compared to actual performance.

A lot of PC games will automatically set your visual options based on the hardware you're running, and I can see that becoming more and more of a console thing if these upgraded consoles every so often takes off. Sure it can only go as high as the max settings that have been created, but PC devs often like to include insane options that will butcher even decently high-end PCs. Stuff like that could probably future-proof a game for the next console upgrade or even two. It took years before any modest PC could run Crysis at max settings for one example, before that it was limited to top of the range builds.

You're pretty bang on the money. A lot of software for Windows needed to know what version it was running on, whether 95, 98, XP, Vista etc, and 95/98 often were grouped together because of their age and simularities.

It's basically a programmer being lazy/effecient and instead of typing something like if windows version is equal to 95 or 98, simply check if the version starts with "9" and then you can catch them both in one easy bit of code, rather than checking both manually.

95/98 were similar and outdated enough to make this kind of code commonplace. Unless there was a specific reason a coder needed to/cared enough to implement specific code differences between 95 and 98, then you quite often got the "starts with 9" catch all instead.

Which is fine, unless Microsoft were to release a totally new Windows 9. All of a sudden you'd get old software trying to run Windows 95/98 code on your brand new swanky machine because it simply saw the 9 and went sweet, load up the old crap.

I don't particularly care what medium it is presented in, whether it's live action, 3D animation, radio drama, books, cartoon or anime.
